attribution: Harvest Brix, titratable acidity (as tartaric) and pH are typical commercial ranges compiled from viticulture and enology extension literature. Four literatures were searched for this cultivar and none carried a usable juice composition table: the California Grape Crush Report, which is scoped to California and does not grow it; PubMed Central, which returns work on phenolics and aroma but no harvest chemistry; the Cornell NYSAES cultivar release bulletins, which cover only varieties Cornell bred; and the NE-1020 multistate wine grape cultivar trial, whose Pennsylvania report does include this cultivar but publishes its Brix, acidity and pH tables as page images, with the prose giving only an aggregate across all cultivars ("titratable acidity between 7.6 and 10.6 g/L", "brix all above 20%"). Sugar is soluble solids times this record's 65% juice yield, the convention this file uses throughout, and ppg is 46 x that.
fermentables.sourceNote:
Two things to know about this figure. It is one site and one vintage, and 2014 was not an ordinary one: the report describes extensive winter injury along Lake Erie, with several cultivars in the same trial producing no fruit at all, so this is a stressed season rather than a typical one.

The report publishes its tables as page images, rotated landscape, so the numbers here came from optical recognition of a scan rather than from a text layer - which is exactly the situation where a column can be misread. fermentables.name: Concord
fermentables.description: Unmistakably foxy from methyl anthranilate, low in sugar and high in acid.
fermentables.usageNotes: Requires substantial chaptalisation. The grape of American grape juice and jelly, and of kosher sweet wine.
fermentables.attribution: No source. An 1849 variety. USDA reports juice-grape tonnage but the Crush Report does not carry it, and nothing published gives per-variety harvest chemistry. The figures here are typical ranges from general viticulture practice rather than a measurement of this cultivar, which is what the previous citation to the UC Davis site amounted to as well — that page 403s to automated requests and its own attribution admitted the numbers were not per-variety. They are declared rather than left looking sourced. Four literatures were searched for this cultivar and none carried a usable juice composition table: the California Grape Crush Report, which is scoped to California and does not grow it; PubMed Central, which returns work on phenolics and aroma but no harvest chemistry; the Cornell NYSAES cultivar release bulletins, which cover only varieties Cornell bred; and the NE-1020 multistate wine grape cultivar trial, whose Pennsylvania report does include this cultivar but publishes its Brix, acidity and pH tables as page images, with the prose giving only an aggregate across all cultivars ("titratable acidity between 7.6 and 10.6 g/L", "brix all above 20%"). The stored figures remain typical ranges from general viticulture practice.

fermentables.name: Norton
fermentables.description: A native American species with genuine tannin, deep colour and no foxiness at all.
fermentables.usageNotes: Very high malic acid — malolactic conversion is essential. Missouri's state grape and phylloxera-immune.
fermentables.attribution: Table 4 of the NE-1020 Wine Grape Cultivar Trial 2014 report (R. Crassweller, Penn State, published by the Pennsylvania Department of Agriculture), berry quality at harvest at the Lake Erie Grape Research and Extension Center. For Norton: pH 3.38, titratable acidity 23.6 g/L and soluble solids 21.58%. Stored previously as pH 3.4, TA 10.5 and 23 °Brix with no citation at all. Sugar is soluble solids times this record's 65% juice yield, the convention this file uses throughout, and ppg is 46 x that.
fermentables.sourceNote:
Two things to know about this figure. It is one site and one vintage, and 2014 was not an ordinary one: the report describes extensive winter injury along Lake Erie, with several cultivars in the same trial producing no fruit at all, so this is a stressed season rather than a typical one.

And it was read by OCR. The report publishes its tables as page images, rotated landscape, so the numbers here came from optical recognition of a scan rather than from a text layer - which is exactly the situation where a column can be misread. The assignment was checked against the report's own prose before anything was written: the text states that titratable acidity ran "between 7.6 and 10.6 g/L" for every cultivar except Norton, which was highest, and that Brix was "all above 20%" except Chancellor. Both statements reproduce exactly from the columns as read - eight cultivars inside 7.6 to 10.6, Norton alone at 23.6, and Chancellor alone below 20 at 18.72 - which is what establishes that the acid column is the acid column. Juice yield, colour and fermentability are not in the table.

fermentables.name: Muscadine
fermentables.description: A different species entirely, with thick slip-skins, large berries and a strong musky aroma.
fermentables.usageNotes: Low sugar and heavy chaptalisation are normal. Extremely disease-resistant in the humid Southeast; Scuppernong is the bronze-skinned form.
fermentables.attribution: Islam et al., "Evaluation of Biochemical Juice Attributes and Color-Related Traits in Muscadine Grape Population", Horticulturae 2021, PMC8156615, published CC BY. Ninety muscadine genotypes - 21 standard cultivars, 60 breeding lines and 9 Vitis x Muscadinia hybrids - measured over three consecutive seasons, 2017 to 2019, on 50 berries per replicate and three replicates per genotype. Total soluble solids averaged 14.4 °Brix across the population, from 7.9 in genotype A18-8-2 to 18.1 in O43-1-1 and the cultivar Scarlett; the record stored 15 °Brix. Juice pH ran from 3.11 to 3.85, against a stored 3 to 3.5. Sugar is Brix times this record's 65% juice yield, the convention this file uses throughout, and ppg is 46 x that.
fermentables.sourceNote: The paper's acidity figures were not taken, and the reason is a unit. It reports acidity as "mg tartaric acid/L" - an average of 3.4 with a range of 2.6 to 4.8 - and 3.4 mg/L is three orders of magnitude below the acidity of any grape juice, so the unit as printed cannot be right. The numbers are almost certainly g/L, which would put muscadine well below the 7 g/L this record stores and would be a real correction. This project does not silently reinterpret a published unit, so the stored acidity is unchanged and remains unsourced. Note also what the population is: mostly breeding lines rather than wine cultivars, and the paper puts the two standard wine cultivars, Noble and Carlos, in its low-sugar group - so 14.4 Brix is the population average, not a winemaking target. Colour, fermentability and juice yield are not from this paper.
